Chunking Strategy: Parent-Child Chunking Strategy (Small-to-Big Retrieval / Auto-Merging Retrieval)
Description: Solves the trade-off in RAG by storing large context units as parents and smaller overlapping slices as children for vector search, decoupling the chunk used for vector similarity retrieval from the chunk used for LLM context to balance precision with broad background context.
Step-by-Step Execution Process:
Pre-process text (e.g., regex via pure Ruby String#gsub) to normalize whitespace and remove bloat like URLs/emails or extract structural blocks. 2. Store each structural or large segment block (e.g., 4,000 characters or Full Doc Mode using hierarchical delimiters like 

, 
, ., ?, !,  ) as a ParentChunk in a fast KV, relational schema (e.g., via sequel), or document database. 3. Further segment those parent blocks into smaller, overlapping token/word windows or child chunks (e.g., 512 characters) using the same recursive delimiter hierarchy. 4. Store and index each smaller window as a ChildChunk in the vector database (e.g., pgvector), attaching a parent_id foreign key reference. 5. Generate vector embeddings (via ruby_llm.embed) for child chunks only. 6. During search, execute vector similarity nearest-neighbor search (<=>) on child chunks to find top-K matches. 7. Map retrieved top-K child chunks back to their distinct parent_id references via SQL JOIN or SELECT IN. 8. Retrieve and send the full corresponding ParentChunk texts to the LLM's context window.
Primary Use Cases: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems needing accurate similarity searches without sacrificing necessary context for comprehensive LLM answers.
Key Advantages: High precision during vector similarity searches using short child chunks, while providing broad, sufficient context to the LLM via encompassing parent chunks.
Correlated Gem / Tool: kreuzberg, tiktoken_ruby, pragmatic_segmenter, pure Ruby (String#gsub), sequel, pgvector, ruby_llm

Description: Embeds an LLM-generated summary of a table as the child chunk while keeping the original structured table as the parent.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Extract table as Markdown or HTML. 2. Store the full Markdown/HTML table in a KV store as the ParentChunk. 3. Send the table to a fast/cheap LLM with a prompt to summarize content, key metrics, and categories. 4. Embed the generated natural language summary as the ChildChunk pointing to the parent_id.
Key Advantages: Converts numeric/tabular grid data into semantic natural language that vector databases can easily match.

Description: Serializes individual rows into self-contained sentences prepended with column headers.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Store the full table (or block of rows) as the ParentChunk. 2. Programmatically iterate through table data and prepend column headers to every cell in a row. 3. Embed each serialized row (or small batch of rows) as a ChildChunk pointing to the parent.
Primary Use Cases: Extremely long tables spanning multiple pages with thousands of rows.
Key Advantages: Prevents context window overflow and preserves tabular row-column associations for massive tables.

Chunking Strategy: Semantic Schema Extraction / Schema-Based Table Retrieval
Description: Embeds the table's structural schema (headers and topic) instead of its raw values to match user query concepts.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Extract column and row headers from the table block using code or an LLM. 2. Generate a 'Schema Signature' string representing the topic and column layout (optionally adding sample row values). 3. Embed the schema signature as the ChildChunk pointing to the parent_id. 4. Retrieve the parent table when a user's query concepts match the embedded schema signature.
Primary Use Cases: Tables used as multi-dimensional summaries; correlatable topic modeling across datasets.
Key Advantages: Preserves multi-dimensional relationships without losing structured schema; enables topic modeling and efficient filtering.

Description: Splits text based on a hierarchy of separators (e.g., paragraphs, sentences, words).
Key Advantages: Preserves semantic boundaries, more natural chunks.

Description: Uses embeddings to identify natural breakpoints and group text fragments based on meaning rather than hard structural rules.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Base Splitting: Uses a fast, small-scale recursive chunker to chop text into atomic units (e.g., single sentences). 2. Embedding: Transforms each atomic sentence into a dense vector using an embedding model. 3. Clustering: Calculates cosine similarity distance between adjacent vectors and iteratively groups them into the same chunk as long as semantic similarity stays above a dynamically calculated threshold.
Key Advantages: Preserves semantic context, better for meaning-based retrieval.

Description: Processes HTML content while preserving structural elements.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Pass raw HTML strings to ruby_llm using ruby_llm-schema to force the LLM to extract and chunk only relevant layout sections.
Primary Use Cases: Web scraping, content extraction from HTML.
Key Advantages: Maintains web content structure, handles nested elements.

Description: Splits text at sentence boundaries.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Pass text directly to PragmaticSegmenter::Segmenter.new(text: text).segment for sentence boundary detection.
Key Advantages: Preserves complete thoughts, good for NLP tasks.

Description: Uses natural paragraph breaks as chunk boundaries.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Execute pure Ruby regex splits text.split(/\n\n+/).
Key Advantages: Maintains natural reading flow, simple to implement.

Description: Uses dependency parsing to identify logical units.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Initialize a ruby-spacy NLP pipeline to extract syntactic dependency trees and group tokens based on root linguistic relationships.
Key Advantages: Preserves grammatical relationships, highly contextual.

Description: Combines multiple strategies (e.g., semantic + structural).
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Split text via pragmatic_segmenter (structural). 2. Dynamically group segments using informers embeddings (semantic).
Key Advantages: Balances structure and meaning preservation.

Description: Creates chunks with overlap between them.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Extract sentences using pragmatic_segmenter. 2. Use pure Ruby array manipulation like sentences.each_cons(3).map(&:join) to create sliding windows.
Key Advantages: Preserves context across chunk boundaries.

Description: Adjusts chunk sizes based on content characteristics.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Leverage dspy.rb using a Predict module and ChainOfThought signature to prompt the LLM to predict and adjust optimal bounds dynamically.
Primary Use Cases: Variable content types, mixed document collections.
Key Advantages: Adapts to document structure, optimizes for meaning.

Description: Uses document sections (like chapters) as primary boundaries.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Extract sections using inkmark for static metadata, or have ruby_llm identify chapter boundaries mapped to a strict schematist.
Key Advantages: Preserves high-level document organization.

Description: Ensures complete entities stay within chunks.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Extract named entities via ruby-spacy and conditionally prevent standard splitting if the boundary index intersects an active entity span.
Primary Use Cases: Named entity recognition tasks, knowledge graphs.
Key Advantages: Maintains entity integrity, better for entity-focused tasks.

Description: Groups content by detected topics.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Apply informers sequence classification models to categorize text segments, or use rubyfca (Formal Concept Analysis) to cluster shared concepts.
Key Advantages: Thematically coherent chunks.

Description: Uses domain-specific rules for chunk boundaries.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Define strict custom domain schemas with dry-types and enforce structured JSON chunk outputs via schmeatist.
Key Advantages: Tailored to specific content types.

Description: Outsources the chunking logic entirely to a Large Language Model.
Step-by-Step Execution Process: Prompting: Full document (or large sliding window) is passed to the LLM. 2. Reasoning: The LLM is instructed to identify major thematic shifts, chapter breaks, or logical topic transitions. 3. Structured Output: Using a strict JSON schema, the LLM outputs exact string indices or literal boundary phrases to split the document.
Primary Use Cases: High-context document splitting where latency and API cost are secondary.
Key Advantages: Perfect contextual boundaries.
